<|channel|>analysis<|message|>We have two papers. Paper1: Enhancing Mobile Voice Assistants with WorldGaze. Paper2: Selecting Real-World Objects via User-Perspective Phone Occlusion.

We need differences in implementations for head-gaze method in user studies between these two papers.

Paper1: in head- gaze method, they use the front camera to track the user's head direction and raycast to rear camera's 3D world. They used only smartphone’s built-in cameras (front+rear). They didn't use head-worn camera. They used ARKit 3's face API to track head pose in 3D, then projected ray.

In Paper2: they proposed occlusion-based method, using front camera for iris tracking (although it says using IR camera? It uses MediaPipe Iris real-time cropping, using front camera to estimate 3D head vector? Actually they use front camera’s iris position and estimate occlusion area. They used an occlusion-based method. In user studies, they used a head-worn camera to measure the ground truth of head orientation. They used a head-worn camera to calibrate the orientation for the head-gaze method, because the results were inaccurate otherwise. They also used a VR environment? For user studies, they used a head-worn camera for accurate measurement of head orientation. The paper's method: the occlusion-based method, they rely on front camera and rear camera to estimate occlusion area. They use the ref side etc. There's a mention of in The Implementation: They used a head-worn camera to measure the ground truth of head orientation. The head-worn camera is not used in the mid-s process? Actually they used the head-worn camera for head-gaze method in the user studies. Yes: In page 5, "M3: Head-Gaze. The user holds the phone in front of the face and uses head orientation as the virtual ray to select targets. The phone’s screen remains dark all the time. This method is a reference to the implementation of WorldGaze [43]. For baseline M1 (Photograph) ... For baseline M3 (Head-Gaze), the users wear the head-worn camera for measuring. This indicates that Paper2 uses head-worn camera in user studies.

Thus differences:

- Paper1 uses smartphone’s built-in front camera to track head pose; no head-worn. Paper2 uses head-worn camera for hand-hold. Additionally, Paper2's head-gaze method is used as a baseline to compare to occlusion, but it uses the head-worn camera for calibration. But the main difference: Paper1 uses front camera inside; Paper2 uses head-worn camera for ground truth. And Paper2 uses occlusion-based method as main technique, not head-gaze beam (though they use head-gaze baseline for comparison).

Thus which option correctly captures the difference? Option C: says Paper1 uses front cameras to track head direction and raycasts to rear camera, uses only smartphone built-in cameras. Paper2 employs a head-worn camera to accurately measure ground truth of head orientation. That matches what we know: Paper2 uses head-worn camera to measure head orientation. Option B: says Paper2 introduces a different approach where both front and rear cameras are used to estimate occlusion area, and then the user's gaze direction can be calculated from the phone's positioning and occlusion area. That also somewhat correct: Paper2 uses front and rear camera to estimate occlusion area. But the focus of the question: differences in implementations for head-gaze method in user studies. That is about head-gaze method; Paper1: head-gaze method (using smartphone cameras). Paper2: head-gaze method used as baseline with head-worn camera. So option C seems more appropriate.

Option D: says Paper2's method refers to implementation of Paper1, while they add an extra camera to phone to measure orientation. That wrong: Paper2 used a head-worn camera for measurement of ground truth, not an extra camera.

So final: Option C.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>\boxed{C}
